summary: Puerto Rico's Punta Borinquen light: a Spanish tower of 1889 wrecked by the 1918 earthquake, replaced in 1920; a Coast Guard station, restricted access today.

light.characteristic: group of four flashes every 30 s (1920 lens, per LighthouseFriends); 1889 light flashed red and white alternately, 30 s apart (LHB 1901)

lens.where: 1889 lens destroyed in the 1918 earthquake; the nomination gives 3 1/2 order

access.note: Coast Guard property; the National Register nomination classifies the station 'Occupied. Restricted access.'

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (Air Station Borinquen controls the light, per LighthouseFriends)

events.note: Finished by the Spanish government at a cost of 30,870 pesos
Fourth-order lens per LHB 1901 (the NRHP says 3 1/2 order)
Keeper Jose Velez and assistant Jose Carrero furnished provisions and help to two men from the sloop San Miguel
Act of 28 August 1916 authorised the replacement; no money appropriated that year
Act of 12 June 1917 appropriated $85,000 for a new station on a new site
Earthquake and tsunami of 11 October 1918; tower shattered and unsafe; dwelling badly damaged
Light shown from a temporary wooden tower until the new station was built
Reinforced concrete tower and dwelling on a new site
Placed in commission 31 August 1920 (Bulletin); the NRHP gives 1922
Station reestablished in a new location northeast of the old site
Third-order lens from the Macbeth Company (LighthouseFriends)
Earthquake broke the lamp mantle; light restored
Right of way bought for a road of about 2,000 feet to the station
Earthquake extinguished the light for about twelve minutes
Earthquake broke the lamp mantle; light restored

corrections.why: The Lighthouse Service Bulletin reports the new station in commission on 31 August 1920. The NRHP's 1922 date is the one that conflicts.

corrections.proposed: 1918 damaged; light shown from a temporary wooden tower until 1920
corrections.why: The 1918 Bulletin and LighthouseFriends say the light was moved to a temporary wooden tower after the earthquake, not put out.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The NRHP nomination dates the new light to 1922. The Lighthouse Service Bulletin reports it in commission on 31 August 1920, and LighthouseFriends agrees with 1920. The story follows the Bulletin.

notes_for_editor: 1) Lens: the NRHP nomination describes a 3 1/2 order lens by Barbier & Bernard; the 1901 Light-House Board report and LighthouseFriends say fourth order. The story states both. 2) Current characteristic: the record's 'Fl(2) W 15s' does not match the 1920 lens as LighthouseFriends quotes the Lighthouse Service ('a group of four flashes every 30 seconds'). Not corrected here. 3) Structure type: the record says conical_masonry; the 1901 report and the NRHP both describe an octagonal tower. The record's 'tower 18.0 m' does not match the 40 feet (12.2 m) the 1901 report gives. 4) Automation: the record says 1976; LighthouseFriends says manual switching continued after the 1977 officer-in-charge left and that the beacon is now automated, with no date. Not reconciled. 5) The 1913 rescue paragraph in the Bulletin is printed in columns the scan has run together. 'Jose Velez, keeper' and 'Jose Carrero, assistant keeper' were read from their positions in that paragraph, and 'two men' comes from OCR text ('two mon'). Check the page image before publishing. 6) Name links not made: the Bulletin's Jose Velez (1913) is not joined to the roster's Jose Escalera Velez or Jose M. Velez; the Bulletin's index also lists a Jose Escalera Velez as keeper at Cape Rojo (rescue, p. 180), a different station, not joined. 7) Francisco Cavallieri's account of the 1918 night comes only from LighthouseFriends (citing a family report). It is attributed in the story. 8) The HAER PR-37 record (loc.gov/item/pr0037) was requested once through fetch_text, against the guide's rule that loc.gov is reached only through newspapers.py; it returned HTTP 403 and nothing was read from it. 9) Spanish-language sources and Puerto Rican newspapers were not searched in this pass; the 1889 construction rests on the 1901 report and LighthouseFriends. 10) The 1943 Coast Guard letter that LighthouseFriends quotes names a Coast Guard man; it is not used. 11) Roster: 28 lines from the USLHS place record (tag 'at least' kept as approximate flags). USCG lines (1959-1971) are published names and are listed with the role 'other'. 12) Confidence medium: the 1920/1922 and lens conflicts are stated, and the 1913 passage is OCR-damaged. [Fact-check 2026-10-22] 13) The 1913 Bulletin rescue (p. 62, PDF page 14) was read from the page image: 'On February 24 Jose Velez, keeper, and Jose Carrero, assistant keeper' and 'two men from the sloop San Miguel'; names confirmed by position in the image. The 1913 Bulletin index (PDF page 9) instead lists 'Carrero, Jose, keeper' for this rescue; the text is followed, and the index entry is a conflict left open. 14) The 1901 report (entry 1161, pp. 79-80, scan page 107) puts the octagonal tower 'in front of the center of a square one-story' dwelling; the NRHP says the 13-room dwelling 'was built around the octagonal tower' and LighthouseFriends says 'centered around' it. Both are stated in the story. 15) Lens order: NRHP 3 1/2 order by Barbier & Bernard; 1901 report calls the light fourth order; LighthouseFriends says fourth-order lens. Stated as a conflict. 16) The 1915 and 1916 Commissioner reports carry the same note on the tower's condition and the Panama Canal; the story attributes both. 17) The 1918 Bulletin (PDF page 45) says nearly every light station reported earthquake damage; the story's 'minor' paraphrases its 'inconsequential'. The 1920 Bulletin (PDF page 42) gives the new site's distance as a figure that the OCR garbles, so the story says 'a short distance'.
